scenes.script: Rome's emperors stop inheriting power. They start being hired by armies.
The Senate still has marble, titles, rituals. The frontier has the swords.
In 235 CE, soldiers murder Severus Alexander and raise Maximinus Thrax.
Maximinus never visits Rome. The capital learns it has become optional.
The old rule is bloodline. The new rule is payroll.
Every frontier has its own emergency: Goths, Franks, Persians, rebels.
One emperor cannot be everywhere. Every general starts looking like a backup emperor.
If a legion feels abandoned, it can simply choose its own savior.
That choice is never symbolic. It comes with twenty thousand armed men.
The pain is simple: loyalty costs more than the treasury can hold.
Each new emperor promises donatives. Each promise teaches the army to ask again.
Assassination becomes succession planning with knives.
More than twenty men claim the purple in less than fifty years.
The empire is still huge. The office at the center becomes too fragile.
Diocletian reads the disaster correctly: one throne is a trap.
He splits power into multiple emperors, courts, armies, and command zones.
Rome survives by building the army directly into the state.
The emperor now stands where the payroll, frontier, and sword all meet.
